Robert W. Service (1874–1958)

🖋️ Pen: tap the two nouns that do an adjective’s job. Ask of each noun: does it tell what kind of thing the next noun is?
The Cremation of Sam McGee
Robert W. Service (1907) · from “The Cremation of Sam McGee,” stanza 11
Sam has died of the cold and made the speaker promise to cremate him. At last the speaker finds an abandoned steamboat jammed in the ice at Lake Lebarge.
· · ·
Some planks I tore from the cabin floor, and I lit the boiler fire; Some coal I found that was lying around, and I heaped the fuel higher; The flames just soared, and the furnace roared—such a blaze you seldom see; And I burrowed a hole in the glowing coal, and I stuffed in Sam McGee.
· · ·
planks: long, flat boards · boiler: the steam tank that drives a steamboat · fuel: anything burned to make heat · seldom: not often · burrowed: dug a hole

3
✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Model
The partners had little money; they bet it all on Buck.

Two complete sentences that belong together can be joined by a semicolon. Buck is a name, so it takes a capital letter.

🔧 Fix this one
the crowd fell silent buck pulled
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

The crowd fell silent; Buck pulled. A period works too: The crowd fell silent. Buck pulled. The sentence opens with a capital, and Buck is a name. These are two complete sentences, so they take a semicolon or a period, never a comma alone.

Next, the chalkboard.

1
🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Nouns that describe, and four marks
Professor Lovelore At the board
1:15
An AI-generated character and voice.
A noun as an adjective
Verb, then subject. Then ask of each noun: what kind? or which one?
The camp fire. What kind of fire? camp.
Camp is still a noun, doing an adjective’s job.
Comma ,
A short pause.
after an opening word or phrase
around an added piece
between items
Semicolon ;
Joins two complete sentences that belong together.
Colon :
After a complete sentence: here it comes.
End marks . ? !
A period, a question mark, an exclamation point. They close a sentence.

6
🪶 Read like a Reader, Read like a Writer, Mimic
One sentence from Chapter VI, three ways.
“Kill or be killed, eat or be eaten, was the law; and this mandate, down out of the depths of Time, he obeyed.”Jack London · The Call of the Wild, Chapter VI
📖 Read like a Reader

What law does the sentence name, and where does it say the law came from? What does it tell you about the way Buck lives?

✏️ Read like a Writer

London joins two sentences with a semicolon, sets an added piece in commas, and puts the object, this mandate, ahead of the verb. What does each choice do to the way the sentence moves?

🖊️ Mimic

Write a sentence in the same shape about a different character: two pairs in the opening, a semicolon, then a second clause with an added piece set off by commas.

___ or ___, ___ or ___, was the rule; and this rule, ___, she followed.

convalescence

ministrations

transient

exploit

incoherent

indiscreet

Your introduction: 4 to 6 sentences
  1. Hook: open with a question, or a moment from the book.
  2. Background: one or two sentences on who Buck was and what has happened to him.
  3. Thesis: end with your claim, stated so clearly that someone could disagree.
4–6 sentences · built from your Lesson 1 outline
🪶 Sentence frames, if you want them

Hook: At ___, Buck was ___. / What would it take for a dog to ___?

Background: Before, Buck ___. By the end of Chapter VI, he ___.

Thesis: Buck’s change ___ because ___.

📖 Priya’s draft, a model
Priya
7th Grade Scholar · an introduction

At Judge Miller’s place, Buck was a proud dog who trusted people and played fair. By the end of Chapter VI, he steals from any camp but one and shows no mercy to a strange dog. Some readers say the North sets Buck free, and his love for John Thornton seems to prove that something good survives. But that love belongs to one man. The North keeps Buck alive, but it destroys most of the fair and trusting dog he was at Judge Miller’s place.
